en: Thus have I heard: the Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta, Discourse on the Lesser Undertaking of Things, from the Majjhima Nikāya, number 45.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of undertaking dharmas.”
Which four?
There is, monks, an undertaking of things that is pleasant in the present and results in suffering in the future;
there is, monks, an undertaking of things that is painful both in the present and results in suffering in the future.
“Monks, there is an undertaking of things that is painful in the present and results in happiness in the future;
there is, monks, an undertaking of things that is pleasant both in the present and results in happiness in the future.
And what, monks, is the undertaking of things that is pleasant in the present and results in suffering in the future?”
“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures.
They fall into a state of being drunk with sensual pleasures.”
They enjoy themselves with female wanderers who wear their hair in topknots.
They say this:
“What future danger do those venerable recluses and brahmins perceive in sensual pleasures that they speak of abandoning them and prescribe the full understanding of sensual pleasures?”
"Happy is the touch of this young female wanderer’s arm, so soft and hairy," they say, and thus they fall into a state of intoxication regarding sensual pleasures.
Having fallen into such intoxication, with the breakup of the body after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
There they experience feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter.
They spoke thus:

“It is because these venerable recluses and brahmins, seeing the future peril in sensual pleasures, have spoken of the abandoning of sensual pleasures and prescribe the full understanding of sensual pleasures;
for it is on account of sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as their cause, that we experience suffering that is sharp and harsh.”
"I am experiencing a bitter sensation.
Monks, it is just as if, in the last month of summer, a *māluva* creeper were to bear fruit,
and then one of its seeds were to fall at the foot of a *sāla* tree.
Then, monks, the deity dwelling in that *sāla* tree would become afraid, agitated, and fall into a state of terror. Then, monks, the friends, companions, kinsmen,
and blood-relatives of that deity dwelling in the *sāla* tree— the deities of the groves, the deities of the woods, the deities of the trees,
and the deities dwelling among the medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants— would gather together and console her thus:
"Do not be afraid, sir; do not be afraid!

Perhaps this *māluva* seed might be swallowed by a peacock, or eaten by a wild animal, or burnt by a forest fire, or pulled out by woodcutters, or an anthill might grow over it, or it might simply perish as a non-seed.
But then, monks, that *māluva* seed was neither swallowed by a peacock, nor eaten by a wild animal, nor burnt by a forest fire... [and so on].
It might burn, yet the foresters would not remove it, nor would termites emerge;
and when that seed is rained upon by a rain-bearing cloud, it would grow properly.
Then that *māluva* creeper—tender, soft, hairy, and trailing—would cling to that *sāla* tree.
Then, monks, it occurred to the deity dwelling in that *sāla* tree:
"What indeed are those worthy friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives— the deities of groves,
deities of forests, deities of trees, and deities dwelling in medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants— who, perceiving the future danger regarding the *māluva* seed, have gathered together..."
Having come together, they comforted him thus:
"Do not fear, sir, do not fear!

Perhaps a peacock might swallow this mālūva seed, or a wild animal might eat it, or a forest fire might burn it, or woodcutters might remove it, or termites might swarm over it, or else it might perish as a non-seed."
‘Pleasant is the touch of this young, soft, hairy, hanging-down māluva creeper.
She would then encircle that sāla tree;
having encircled the sāla tree, she would form a canopy above it.
Having built a platform on top, one would cause a flood to arise.
Having caused the flood to arise, one would split apart the very large trunks of that sal tree.
Then, monks, the deity dwelling in that sal tree would think thus:

“Indeed, sirs, these friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives of yours—the deities dwelling in groves, the deities dwelling in forests, the deities dwelling in trees, and the deities dwelling in medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants—perceiving the future danger regarding this *māluva* seed, have gathered together and consoled you thus:
‘Do not fear, sir; do not fear, sir! Perhaps a peacock might swallow this *māluva* seed, or perhaps a deer...’”
"Or it might be eaten, or a forest fire might burn it, or woodcutters might clear it away, or termites might raise up,
or it might perish as seed. "And yet,
because of this *māluva* seed, I am experiencing painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations."
In the same way, monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this: “There is no fault in sensual pleasures.
They fall into the habit of drinking in sensual pleasures;
they amuse themselves with female wanderers wearing hair-ornaments.
They spoke thus:

“What future danger do those venerable recluses and brahmins perceive regarding sensual pleasures that they speak of abandoning sensual pleasures and prescribe the full understanding of sensual pleasures?
Pleasant is the touch of this young female wanderer’s arm—so tender and soft with down!”
They fall into a state of being drunk with sensual pleasures.
Having fallen into a state of being drunk with sensual pleasures, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
There they experience feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter.
They spoke thus:

“It is because these venerable recluses and brahmins, perceiving the future peril in sensual pleasures, have spoken of the abandoning of sensual pleasures and prescribe the full understanding of sensual pleasures.
For it is on account of sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as their cause, that we experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings.”
This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future.
And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is painful both in the present and results in suffering in the future?

Here, monks, a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; he does not accept food brought to him, nor food specially prepared for him, nor an invitation.
He does not accept [food] from the mouth of a jar, nor from the mouth of a basket;

he does not accept it with a sheep’s fleece between, nor with a staff between, nor with a pestle between; he does not accept it from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing, nor from a woman in the presence of her husband, nor from groups of people, nor from where a dog is waiting, nor from where flies are swarming.
Moving from house to house, he does not eat fish, nor meat, nor drink fermented liquor, spirits, or grain-beer.
He may live at a single house, taking a single morsel of food; or he may live at two houses, taking two morsels; ... up to ... seven houses, taking seven morsels.
He subsists on one alms-gift, or he subsists on two alms-gifts; ... up to ... he subsists on as many as seven alms-gifts.

He takes food once a day, or he takes food once every two days... or he takes food once every seven days. Thus, in such a manner, he dwells devoted to the practice of taking meals at intervals, even up to once a fortnight.

He becomes one who eats greens, or one who eats millet, or one who eats wild rice, or one who eats the *daddula* grain, or one who eats *haṭa* grass, or one who eats husks, or one who eats the scum of boiled rice, or one who eats oil-cake.
Or he is one who eats grass, or one who eats cow dung, or he subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating only what falls [of its own accord].
He wears hempen garments, or garments of hemp-mixed cloth, or shrouds from a cemetery, or rag-robes, or bark garments,
or antelope skins, or strips of antelope skin, or clothes made of kusa grass.
He wears a garment of bark, he wears a garment of wood-shavings, he wears a blanket of human hair,
he wears a blanket of animal fur, he wears an owl’s wing;
he is one who plucks out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out his hair and beard.
He is one who stands continuously; he rejects sitting down;
he squats, devoted to the exertion of squatting;
he uses a bed of thorns, spreading his sleep upon a bed of thorns.
He dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water for a third time each day.
Thus, he dwells devoted to various kinds of such practices involving the mortification and tormenting of the body.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even hell.
This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present and results in suffering in the future.
And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future?
Here, monks, a certain person is by nature intensely passionate; he constantly experiences the pain and mental distress born of passion.
By nature he is prone to intense hatred, and thus he constantly experiences suffering and mental distress born of hatred;
by nature he is prone to intense delusion, and thus he constantly experiences suffering and mental distress born of delusion.
Yet, even with such suffering and mental distress, even weeping with a tearful face, he leads the complete and pure holy life.
Thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future.
And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant both in the present and results in happiness in the future?
In this case, monks, a certain person by nature is not prone to intense lust; he does not constantly experience the suffering and dejection born of lust.
By nature he is not prone to intense hatred; he does not constantly experience the suffering and dejection born of hatred.
By nature he is not prone to intense delusion; he does not constantly experience the suffering and dejection born of delusion.

Thus, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
… [and so on] … the third jhāna.
He enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future.
“These, monks, are the four ways of undertaking things.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Shorter Discourse on Undertaking Dhamma, the fifth, is finished.
